KEY MESSAGE 1...The remnants of Isaias Sunday and Sunday night 
brings rain, some potentially heavy at times, gusty winds and a low 
risk for an isolated severe thunderstorm.

A closed mid level low and surface low, the remnants of former 
Hurricane Isaias, is forecast to slide across the Mid-Atlantic 
region Sunday night into early Monday morning. As this occurs, it is 
forecast to weaken further with the closed mid level low opening up 
more into a trough. The main impacts for our area will be widespread 
rainfall and some gusty winds.

Large scale ascent will start to increase from the south late 
tonight as the system approaches. An east to southeast robust low-
level jet (around 925 mb) on the order of 40-60 knots will 
overspread our area Sunday morning and this will rapidly increase 
the warm air advection initially above a marine stable layer. This 
will enhance the lift (strong 700-850 mb frontogenesis) as the low 
to mid level flow veers with height. In addition, deeper moisture 
will be advected northward into our area with this peaking Sunday 
afternoon into the evening as a warm sector gradually advects 
northward. The precipitable water values are forecast to quickly 
increase from south to north late tonight through Sunday to 1.75-
2.25 inches. As this coincides with strong forcing for ascent 
Sunday, some periods of heavier rain should occur. Total rainfall 
amounts still look to be 1-2 inches across the entire area, however 
up to 3 inches will be possible where some enhancement and/or 
embedded convective elements occur. This event should initially be 
in the form of stratiform rain before transitioning to more 
convective/showery Sunday night into early Monday morning. WPC has 
maintained most of the region in a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) 
for excessive rainfall for Sunday into Sunday night, which means 
isolated instances of flash flooding will be possible. There are 
currently no river gauges forecast to reach minor flood stage, 
however if even heavier rain occurs into northern NJ (especially 
2.5+ inches), this could cause some gauges in the Raritan basin (the 
Millstone River) to rise to minor flood stage. If rainfall rates 
become high enough for a time, then some urban/roadway flooding will 
also be possible.

As the low-level jet moves across the area and the warm sector 
gradually spreads northward on Sunday, an easterly wind will 
increase and become gusty. Where the better warm sector gets, the 
surface winds will veer more out of the southeast to south with 
time. The surface wind speeds will be driven by how much mixing 
occurs within the boundary layer, and this looks to be greatest 
along the coast given the onshore wind and warmer ocean allowing for 
a bit more mixing onto the adjacent land. There is a robust wind 
field forecast to be in place not to far above the surface, however 
a moist/stable layer should keep this from fully mixing down. Wind 
gusts up to 30 mph are anticipated inland with gusts up to 40 mph 
along the coast. The winds should diminish Sunday night as the 
remnant surface low slides across our area and the low-level jet 
shifts away from our region.

While this is the remnants of a tropical system, it has had plenty 
of time being a post-tropical system prior to reach our area. 
Nevertheless, low-level shear profiles increase quite a bit for a 
time Sunday into Sunday evening. For awhile there will be a marine 
influence given the onshore flow and with a period of stratiform 
rain this will keep the instability limited to near zero. However, 
as the main rain shield starts to shift north and east of our area 
either later Sunday afternoon and/or Sunday evening, some 
instability may try to advect northward across Delmarva into 
southern New Jersey especially. Model forecast soundings show the 
flow veering with time and this would weaken the low-level 
shear/helicity (spin). There appears to be a very small window of 
opportunity though in Delmarva where lingering stronger deep-layer 
shear overlaps with some increase in instability for perhaps a few 
transient low-topped supercells with an isolated damaging wind gust 
possible. The severe scenario however is highly contingent on how 
much higher dew points advect northward with enough low-level 
instability, and this looks to be greater to our south and 
southwest. The risk for a weak/brief tornado in our area is 
therefore very low.

Some showers linger early Monday morning, especially from about the 
I-95 corridor on south and east, then drying should quickly occur 
during Monday as a north to northwest wind increases for a time and 
the entire weakening system exits to our east and northeast.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Minor tidal flooding possible with Sunday morning's
high tide, mainly for coastal areas within Delaware Bay. A Coastal
Flood Advisory is in effect for Kent County, DE. 

With a period of east/southeasterly flow expected and the 
upcoming New Moon, increased tidal levels are expected
